n: In this lesson we study haemotropic poisons. The plan has six parts. First, haemotropic poisons, their classification and practical importance are considered. Then the mechanism of action and clinical picture of carbon monoxide, next the post-mortem signs and preliminary tests, then quantitative analysis and its limitations. The fifth part is methaemoglobin: the substances that form it, the clinical picture and post-mortem changes. Finally we compare the two groups, solve the teaching cases and answer the review questions.

The first section: haemotropic poisons, in brief. Haemotropic poisons act primarily on the composition of the blood. That is, their main harm is directed precisely at the blood. In the text these poisons are divided into five groups. In practice haemoglobinotropic substances are encountered more often. Haemoglobinotropics include carbon monoxide and substances that form methaemoglobin. Remember the questions and answers in the table in this order, because the following parts are devoted to precisely these two groups.

Now the classification of haemotropic poisons. In the text they are divided into five groups. The first group acts on haemopoiesis: this includes benzene, lead compounds and cytostatics. The second group causes haemagglutination: ricin and phasin. The third acts on blood coagulation: snake venoms and dicoumarin. The fourth are those causing haemolysis: arsine and amanitohaemolysin. The fifth group is the haemoglobinotropics, which include carbon monoxide and methaemoglobin formers. The main topic of this lesson is precisely this last group.

Now blood poisons according to Table 6.1. This is the classification of V.L. Popov, dating from 1990. In the table poisons are divided into three groups. The haemoglobinotropic group includes carboxyhaemoglobin formers, methaemoglobin formers and others. In the haemolytic group stand arsine, acetic acid and copper sulphate. Among other blood poisons are ricin, phasin, dicoumarin, benzene and cytostatics. It can be seen that this classification groups the division of the previous slide differently, in table form.

The second section: carbon monoxide, in brief. Carbon monoxide is a colourless, odourless gas that forms carboxyhaemoglobin. The main mechanism is this: hypoxia develops through carboxyhaemoglobin. The gas forms when organic substances burn incompletely. The colour of the body is pinkish-red. In the preliminary examination alkali and spectroscopic tests are used. Confirmation, however, is obtained by quantitative spectrophotometry. Thus the preliminary test and the confirmatory method differ from each other; remember this.

The properties of carbon monoxide and the circumstances of poisoning. Carbon monoxide forms when organic substances burn incompletely; it is a colourless, odourless gas. Poisoning is observed in fires, near faulty heating stoves, and next to a running engine in an unventilated building. As to circumstances, poisoning is mainly an accident and occasionally occurs as suicide. Because the gas is odourless, a person may not notice the danger, so knowledge of the conditions at the scene is important for the expert.

The mechanism of action of carbon monoxide. At its base lies formation of carboxyhaemoglobin. The process runs in sequence. First carbon monoxide combines with haemoglobin. As a result COHb forms. After that the blood loses its ability to carry oxygen. Eventually hypoxia develops. That is, haemoglobin binds carbon monoxide instead of oxygen and tissues are left without oxygen. This chain must be remembered in its sequence.

t: Carbon monoxide: effect on tissue respiration
n: Carbon monoxide also affects tissue respiration, because iron-containing systems are damaged too. The objects of action: cytochrome and cytochrome oxidase, catalase and peroxidase, and also myoglobin. As a result tissue respiration is weakened, especially in the brain. In large concentration the central nervous system is paralysed. In addition, capillary permeability increases. Thus carbon monoxide harms not only haemoglobin but also the iron-containing enzymes of the tissues.

t: Carbon monoxide: elimination and time of sampling
n: The elimination of carbon monoxide affects the time of sampling. Carbon monoxide is not metabolised in the body and is eliminated through the lungs. In fresh air it is completely eliminated in a few hours. The practical consequence is this: the blood sample is taken as early as possible. For if it is delayed, the amount of carboxyhaemoglobin may fall and the analytical result will not show the true state. Therefore the time of sampling is a decisive factor for the expert.

The clinical stages of carbon monoxide poisoning. Signs usually develop gradually. The first stage is onset: headache, tinnitus and vomiting. In the second stage the circulation changes: the face reddens and the pulse quickens. In the third stage muscles and breathing are disturbed: weakness and disordered breathing are observed. The fourth stage is coma: consciousness is lost and convulsions appear. That is, poisoning passes gradually from mild signs to a severe state.

Complication and the fulminant form. A severe complication is toxic cerebral oedema, while central hyperthermia is regarded as an early sign. At large concentration the fulminant form develops. Here the concentration in the air is above 1 %. Consciousness is lost quickly, isolated convulsions are observed and breathing stops within a few seconds. An important point: COHb is found only in the blood of the left ventricle and aorta. This means that death is so rapid that the gas has no time to spread through all the blood.

The carboxyhaemoglobin values are given in the textbook. The first signs appear at 25–30 % COHb. Death, that is, paralysis of the respiratory centre, occurs at a level above 60 %. At a concentration of 0.4 % in the air, death is seen within 20–30 min. The fulminant form develops at a concentration in the air above 1 %. Remember: against a background of disease, death is possible even at a lower level. Therefore these figures should be taken not as an absolute limit but as the textbook values.

Signs of carbon monoxide in the body: colour. COHb and carboxymyoglobin are pinkish-red. Therefore cadaveric lividity has a pinkish-red tint. Muscles and heart cavities are also this colour. Blood in the vessels is fluid and of this colour. Internal organs also have this colour. This colour is sometimes seen on the skin and mucous membranes. That is, the pinkish-red colour appears as a sign spread throughout the body.

t: Carbon monoxide: the body, internal organs
n: Changes in the internal organs of the body. Changes differ according to the duration of poisoning. General findings: congestion of the brain and internal organs, small haemorrhages found under the serosa and in the intestinal mucosa. In prolonged cases symmetrical necrosis appears in the subcortical nuclei. Degeneration and necrotic change are seen in the heart, liver and kidney. Thus the longer the poisoning drags on, the deeper the changes in the organs.

Preliminary tests: alkali methods. The Hoppe-Seyler and Liebmann tests are based on colour. When alkali or formaldehyde is added to normal blood, alkaline or formalin haematin forms and the colour turns brown, brownish-black. If these reagents are added to blood containing COHb, the colour of the blood does not change. That is, if the colour does not change, this points to the presence of carbon monoxide. These methods are simple and serve for a preliminary conclusion.

Preliminary test: spectroscopy. Oxy- and carboxyhaemoglobin each have two absorption bands. In normal blood two bands are seen in the yellow-green region. If sodium hydrosulphite is added, reduced haemoglobin forms and the band becomes one. In blood containing COHb there are also two bands in the yellow-green region. But when hydrosulphite is added the two bands remain unchanged. The difference is here: in normal blood the band merges, while in blood containing COHb it does not change.

The place of preliminary tests. These tests are used in examination of the body and in the clinic. They do not require complex equipment. The task of the test is to detect the presence of COHb preliminarily. However, quantitative spectrophotometry is necessary to confirm the diagnosis. This means that a simple test gives only direction, and final confirmation is obtained by precise quantitative analysis.

Interpreting the confirmatory result. A critical approach to results is required. A low or negative result is possible. The reasons: in rapid death the poison acted directly on the brain, or the person was in fresh air before death. Practical conclusion: the result is treated critically, and the blood sample is taken as early as possible and immediately on arrival at the institution. That is, a low figure does not exclude poisoning.

The third section: methaemoglobin, in brief. Methaemoglobin is a brown derivative of haemoglobin. It is formed by nitrite, nitrate, nitrobenzene and aniline. The main harm is that oxygen is not carried; this is called haemic hypoxia. The first signs appear when MetHb exceeds 30 %. The lethal level occurs when MetHb exceeds 70 %. The cadaveric lividity is bluish-grey, brown. Remember these figures in the order of the table.

Methaemoglobin-forming substances. They fall into four groups. The first group is nitrate and nitrite salts, of which nitrite acts more strongly. The second group is nitrogenous aromatic compounds: nitrobenzene and aniline. The third group is potassium chlorate, that is, Berthollet's salt. The fourth group includes hydroquinone. Thus these substances, although different in chemical structure, lead to the same result, that is, formation of methaemoglobin.

Occurrence of methaemoglobin-forming substances. These substances are used in industry and medicine. In industry they are met with in rubber and dye manufacture. In food they are used in preparing canned meat. In medicine they are also used in medical practice. Poisoning has been relatively rare in recent times. As to circumstances, it is usually an accident. That is, the danger remains present in industrial and domestic settings.

The nature of methaemoglobin. Methaemoglobin is a derivative of haemoglobin, brown in colour. In it the iron is held firmly in the trivalent state, that is, trivalent iron is bound to hydroxyl. The consequence is that methaemoglobin cannot bind oxygen. As a result oxygen is not carried to the tissues. Thus the basis of poisoning is linked with a change in the valency of iron, which nullifies the main function of haemoglobin.

Haemolysis at large concentration. When methaemoglobin is at large concentration, haemolysis begins. The process runs as follows: first the resistance of erythrocytes falls. Then haemolysis occurs, that is, breakdown of erythrocytes. Finally anaemia and methaemoglobinuria appear. This chain shows that poisoning with methaemoglobin formers proceeds not only with hypoxia but also with damage to blood cells.

Methaemoglobin: concentration and clinical picture. Signs of haemic hypoxia are mainly observed. When methaemoglobin exceeds 30 %, the first signs appear. Above 70 %, death occurs. Clinically, dyspnoea, cyanosis and headache occur. Dizziness and collapse then join. Remember: these figures differ from the carboxyhaemoglobin values; they must not be mixed up.

Substance-specific actions. In poisoning, additional actions occur depending on the substance. Aniline paralyses the respiratory centre. Hydroquinone also paralyses the respiratory centre. Nitrites dilate vessels and lower pressure. Nitrates act only when they are converted to nitrite in the intestine, so their strength is weaker than that of nitrites. That is, to the main haemic hypoxia is added the specific action of the substance itself, altering the clinical picture.

Methaemoglobin: time course. On the first day death is from haemic hypoxia; this is death from acute haemic hypoxia. In subsequent days acute renal failure is responsible. After 1–2 days anaemia and nephrosis with haemoglobinuria develop. In this period MetHb may not be detected in the blood. In severe poisoning, however, MetHb may be found for 5–6 days. This means that the analytical result must be assessed together with the time elapsed.

Liver and kidney damage. When poisoning is more prolonged, damage associated with haemolysis appears. The liver enlarges. The skin and mucous membranes turn yellow. In the kidney oliguria and anuria are observed. That is, the products formed as a result of haemolysis burden these organs and disrupt their function. For this reason, in prolonged cases special attention is paid to changes in these organs.

t: Methaemoglobin: the body, colour and organs
n: Methaemoglobin: colour and organs in the body. The colour inclines to brownish-brown shades. Cadaveric lividity is bluish-grey, brown, dark brown. The internal organs have a brownish tint. The blood is relatively thick and brown. The liver is enlarged, with degeneration. The kidney is also enlarged, its layers not distinguishable. In contrast to the pinkish-red colour of carbon monoxide, here the brown tint is the main sign.

Methaemoglobin: microscopy and odour. An odour characteristic of the substance may be detected. On microscopy of the kidney, nephrosis with haemoglobinuria is found. Nitrobenzene has a bitter almond odour. Aniline has a distinctive aromatic odour. The source of the odour is the body cavities and internal organs. Thus odour helps in suggesting the substance, and microscopy confirms the change in the kidney.

Diagnosis of methaemoglobin. The quality and quantity of methaemoglobin are determined in the blood. Diagnosis rests on three directions. The first is the circumstances of the incident. The second is clinical and morphological signs. The third is determination of MetHb in the blood, using spectrophotometric and gas chromatographic methods. That is, the conclusion rests not only on the laboratory result but on assessment together with the circumstances and morphological signs.

Teaching case one: a closed garage. This is a hypothetical case, not a real examination. Given: found next to a running engine in a closed garage. Cadaveric lividity is pinkish-red. Blood is fluid, muscles pinkish-red. There are small haemorrhages in the brain. There are three questions. Which group of poisons is suspected? What preliminary test is possible? What is needed for confirmation? Think about the answer; we will check it in the next part.

The answer to the first case: carbon monoxide. The set of signs corresponds to carbon monoxide. The most suitable poison is carbon monoxide, that is, carbon(II) oxide. The reason is the pinkish-red lividity and fluid blood. As a preliminary test, an alkali or spectroscopic test is used. For confirmation, quantitative spectrophotometry is needed. Note: a low or negative result is possible. Therefore the result must be viewed critically.

Teaching case two: chemical manufacture. This too is a hypothetical case, not a real examination. Given: a worker engaged in dye manufacture. Dyspnoea, cyanosis and dizziness were observed. Cadaveric lividity is bluish-brown. The blood is brown, with a bitter almond odour. Questions: which group of poisons does it correspond to? What sign distinguishes it from cyanide? What is determined in the blood? First answer yourself.

The answer to the second case: a methaemoglobin-forming substance. The signs correspond to methaemoglobin formers. The most suitable group is MetHb formers, for example nitrobenzene. The difference from cyanide: the blood is brown, whereas with cyanide it is cherry-reddish. With nitrobenzene the odour persists longer. In the blood the quality and quantity of MetHb are determined. In the kidney, nephrosis with haemoglobinuria is found. That is, colour, odour and clinical picture together point to the right group.

Conclusion: we compare carbon monoxide and methaemoglobin. In carbon monoxide, carboxyhaemoglobin forms; in methaemoglobin, MetHb with trivalent iron. The first signs appear with carbon monoxide at 25–30 % COHb, with methaemoglobin when MetHb exceeds 30 %. Death occurs with carbon monoxide at a level above 60 %, with methaemoglobin above 70 %. Cadaveric lividity is pinkish-red with carbon monoxide, bluish-grey, brown with methaemoglobin. In the laboratory, tests and spectrophotometry are used for carbon monoxide, and spectrophotometry and GC for methaemoglobin.

The review questions rest on the review questions of the textbook. Into which groups are haemotropic poisons divided? What changes are found in the body in carbon monoxide poisoning? What are the preliminary tests based on? Why may COHb be low? What is the mechanism of poisoning with methaemoglobin? Answer these questions yourself; it will reinforce the main points of this lesson.
